subject: Paediatrics
summary: Follow‑up is the systematic reassessment of a child after an acute or chronic condition to detect relapse, complications, growth issues and treatment side‑effects, especially where investigations are limited.

sections.p: A follow‑up visit is a planned re‑evaluation of a paediatric patient after discharge or after initiating therapy, aiming to confirm resolution, monitor for recurrence and adjust management.
b: Scheduled within 1–2 weeks for severe infections, 4–6 weeks for surgical wounds, 3–6 months for chronic diseases.
Based on clinical criteria (symptom resolution, growth parameters) and available investigations.

sections.p: Severity is judged by the original disease stage and by any new complications that arise during the interval.
b: Mild: asymptomatic, normal growth, no new signs.
Moderate: intermittent symptoms, minor lab abnormalities.
Severe: persistent fever, organ dysfunction, worsening growth.

sections.p: Re‑presentation can be due to incomplete treatment, drug resistance, co‑infection, malnutrition, or socio‑environmental factors.
b: Inadequate antimicrobial course – common for pneumonia, sepsis.
Malaria relapse or reinfection in endemic areas.
HIV‑related opportunistic infection.
Poor adherence to nutrition or chronic disease regimens.

sections.p: Children may return with fever, worsening cough, diarrhoea, failure to thrive, or new organ‑specific signs.
b: Persistent fever >38 °C after 48 h of therapy.
Weight loss >5 % of baseline.
New skin lesions, joint swelling, or respiratory distress.

t.b: Is there ongoing infection or anaemia? – Elevated WBC or falling haemoglobin suggests unresolved infection or malaria.
Is malaria present? – Positive line confirms infection; negative with high suspicion warrants microscopy.
Is renal function deteriorating? – Rising creatinine indicates AKI or CKD progression.
Is there residual pneumonia or pleural effusion? – Persistent infiltrates or fluid suggest incomplete resolution.
Is growth on track? – Falling below the 5th percentile signals chronic disease or malnutrition.

sections.p: Identify early signs of deterioration that demand urgent referral.
b: Persistent fever >38.5 °C after 72 h of appropriate therapy.
New onset seizures, altered consciousness, or severe dehydration.
Rapid weight loss >10 % in 2 weeks.
Signs of organ failure: jaundice, oliguria, severe tachypnoea.

sections.p: Adjust treatment based on findings, reinforce supportive care, and address barriers to adherence.
b: Complete or change antimicrobial regimen if culture or clinical failure.
Add antimalarial if relapse confirmed.
Provide oral rehydration salts, zinc, and nutrition counselling.
Avoid NSAIDs in children with renal impairment; use paracetamol for fever.
Educate caregivers on drug timing, storage, and when to return.

sections.p: Plan the next review according to disease trajectory and resource availability.
b: Acute infection: review in 7–10 days; if stable, extend to 4 weeks.
Chronic disease (e.g., sickle cell, HIV): clinic every 3 months, with labs at each visit.
Vaccination updates and health‑education sessions at each contact.

sections.p: Distinguish routine follow‑up from acute re‑admission.
b: Re‑admission: new emergency presentation needing inpatient care.
Outpatient review: scheduled, non‑emergent assessment.
Normal haemoglobin may mask early iron deficiency; check ferritin if possible.
Negative malaria RDT can be false‑negative early in infection; repeat if fever persists.
Creatinine may appear normal in children with low muscle mass; use cystatin C if available.

whenToSeekHelp: New seizures or loss of consciousness

faq.q: How often should a child with uncomplicated pneumonia be reviewed?
faq.a: Usually at 48–72 h to ensure clinical improvement, then again at 2 weeks if symptoms persist.

faq.q: What is the best way to monitor growth when scales are unavailable?
faq.a: Use mid‑upper arm circumference and compare to age‑specific reference charts.

faq.q: When can NSAIDs be safely used in children after an infection?
faq.a: Only if renal function is normal and there is no active gastrointestinal bleeding; otherwise prefer paracetamol.

exam: A 4‑year‑old with severe malaria returns 2 weeks after discharge with fever and pallor – what is your next step? — Check haemoglobin and repeat malaria test; treat if positive, otherwise investigate for anaemia causes.
During a follow‑up of a child post‑pneumonia you hear dullness over the left flank – what does this suggest? — Possible pleural effusion; obtain chest X‑ray or bedside ultrasound if available.

A child with sickle cell disease is seen 3 months after starting hydroxyurea and has mild neutropenia; how do you manage? — Continue drug, repeat count in 2 weeks; if neutrophils <0.5 ×10⁹/L stop and refer.

You are in a rural clinic without laboratory support; a child with persistent cough is due for a follow‑up. Which clinical sign will guide you most? — Presence of crackles and oxygen saturation <92 % indicates need for referral.

A caregiver reports that the child’s weight has dropped from the 50th to the 10th percentile in 1 month. What should you prioritize? — Assess for malnutrition, infection, and adherence; start therapeutic feeding and investigate cause.

After a surgical repair of an inguinal hernia, the child presents 6 weeks later with a tender swelling at the scar. What is the likely diagnosis and immediate action? — Likely recurrence or infection; examine, order ultrasound if possible, and arrange surgical review.

During routine follow‑up of an HIV‑positive child, the CD4 count is unchanged but the viral load is rising. What does this indicate? — Treatment failure; consider resistance testing and switch antiretroviral regimen.
A child on long‑term steroids for nephrotic syndrome presents for follow‑up; what monitoring is essential? — Blood pressure, growth, serum glucose, and urine protein; adjust steroid dose accordingly.
